response: {"text":"The research compared recurring motifs in artwork created by service members who have stress‑related, brain‑injury, and other psychological health issues, linking those motifs to standard symptom questionnaires. It was an observational correlation study carried out at a specialized military medical facility. About 370 active‑duty personnel who had experienced head injury, stress symptoms, and related conditions participated. During the first week of a four‑week art‑therapy program they made mask‑like pieces. investigators examined how visual elements—such as signs of mental injury, military symbols, personal identity cues, nature or cultural metaphors, and color symbolism—related to scores on questionnaires measuring stress, depression, and anxiety. Results showed that images portraying psychological injury were associated with higher stress and depression scores, whereas depictions of unit identity, natural or cultural symbols corresponded to lower scores. Fragmented symbols and certain color uses were linked to higher anxiety and mood scores. These visual patterns may give clinicians useful clues about resilience and risk."}
